content: It is a standard parameter included in a complete blood count (CBC) test. In patients with anemia, the MCV value is critical for classifying the anemia as either microcytic (MCV below the normal range) or macrocytic (MCV above the normal range). The MCV is calculated by dividing the hematocrit (the proportion of blood volume occupied by red blood cells) by the red blood cell count (the number of red blood cells per liter of blood). The result is expressed in femtoliters (fL). When the MCV is determined using automated laboratory equipment, it is important to cross-check the result with the red blood cell morphology observed on a peripheral blood smear. Any discrepancies between the automated MCV value and the smear findings may indicate either a malfunction in the equipment or an error by the laboratory technician. The normal reference range for MCV is typically between 80 and 96 fL. However, certain conditions can cause deviations from this range. For example, in hemolytic anemia, the presence of reticulocytes (immature red blood cells) can lead to an increased MCV. In pernicious anemia, which is a type of macrocytic anemia, the MCV can rise significantly, sometimes reaching values as high as 150 fL. An elevated MCV is also commonly associated with chronic alcohol consumption. In such cases, other findings, such as an elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) level and an aspartate aminotransferase (AST) to alanine aminotransferase (ALT) ratio of 2:1, may also be present. Additionally, vitamin B12 deficiency is a well-known cause of macrocytic anemia, characterized by high MCV values. On the other hand, microcytic anemia, which is associated with a low MCV, is most commonly caused by iron deficiency. This may result from insufficient dietary iron intake, gastrointestinal blood loss, or menstrual blood loss. Other common causes of microcytic anemia include thalassemia and chronic diseases. In cases of iron deficiency anemia, the MCV can drop to as low as 60 to 70 fL. In patients with thalassemia, the MCV may also be low, even if the patient does not have iron deficiency. Furthermore, a low MCV in a patient with a positive stool guaiac test (indicating the presence of blood in the stool) is highly suggestive of gastrointestinal cancer.
